content_summary: Per the Crossref abstract: the chapter 'develops an integrated theoretical framework for urban finance based on the generalised benefit principle, building on classical and modern contributions from Wicksell to Stiglitz.' It reviews benefit-taxation models including land value taxation, congestion pricing, and self-financing conditions, and states it identifies their 'limitations in addressing indirect benefits, externalities, and redistributive concerns.' It proposes a 'unified analytical model' linking public-goods provision, congestion effects, land-value gains, and revenue mobilisation, and states it derives conditions for efficient pricing, cost recovery, and fiscal sustainability. It explicitly says it 'synthesises insights from the Henry George theorem, Mohring–Harwitz congestion pricing, and the Wicksellian Connection' and closes with a 'policy-orientated toolbox of revenue instruments.' No numerical results, no India-specific figures, and no explicit statement of what the stated 'limitations' actually are appear in the abstract — those would only surface in the full chapter, which was not accessible.
existing_wiki_coverage: concepts/henry-george-theorem.md (from the corpus digest) already covers Arnott & Stiglitz's canonical formalization, Stiglitz (1977)'s naming, Behrens/Kanemoto/Murata's second-best extension, Tideman's four practical preconditions, and Feldstein's incidence critique — but has no existing mention of Wicksell, the 'Wicksellian Connection,' or Mohring–Harwitz congestion pricing, and no dedicated benefit-principle concept page exists anywhere in the wiki (confirmed by grep across concepts/ and research/). concepts/congestion-pricing.md exists as a separate page this chapter's abstract also touches but does not name specific mechanisms for.
uncertainties: The chapter itself is unread; the abstract's claimed 'limitations' of existing benefit-taxation models (the specific caveats a wiki entry would most want) are named as a topic but not stated in the abstract's text, so nothing about them can be written without fabrication. Whether the 'unified analytical model' is a genuine theoretical advance or a textbook-level restatement cannot be judged from an abstract alone. The book is not yet published (Oct 2026), so no paid-access route exists yet either; a future pass after publication may get further via a library or author copy.

content_summary: Per the Crossref abstract: the chapter 'examines land and property taxation as instruments of benefit taxation and evaluates their role in strengthening municipal finance in India,' set against 'severe fiscal constraints faced by urban local bodies.' It states India's property tax shows 'low yield relative to potential and international benchmarks' (no percentage figures given in the abstract itself). It develops 'an analytical framework linking property tax revenues to tax rates, coverage, valuation, and enforcement efficiency' and reviews 'international practices and valuation methods.' Drawing on 'traditional, capital, and benefit views' of property-tax incidence, it argues property tax is 'an appropriate mechanism for financing local public services,' and it 'reviews reform experiences from Indian cities such as Patna, Hyderabad, and Bengaluru' before concluding that 'comprehensive, system-based property tax reforms grounded in the benefit principle can enhance revenue mobilisation, accountability, and efficiency.' title: Till Gross & Paul Klein, "A new partial-equilibrium approach to approximating the welfare effects of market power and taxes," Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, 2026
what_was_fetched: Crossref carries no abstract for this record (Elsevier withholds it there). DuckDuckGo HTML search snippets located Till Gross's own academic homepage (sites.google.com/site/tillgrosshomepage/research, found after Carleton University's faculty-profile page named him and a search for his personal site resolved through a squatted tillgross.com domain before the correct sites.google.com URL was found via search snippets). That homepage lists this paper as 'accepted at Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization' with a Google-Drive-hosted PDF link. The PDF (file id 1rZnTl6DFfL98HbiAVsqXkOrUy6JEoW1C) was downloaded directly via a `drive.google.com/uc?export=download` URL — no CAPTCHA or auth wall — yielding a complete 37-page working paper (first draft 17 May 2023, this version 16 June 2025), saved at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-georgism-wiki/27113c0d-0e4a-5705-a87d-69e4d8108829/scratchpad/t0-2026-09-27/gross_klein_wp.pdf, and extracted to full text with PyMuPDF at .../gross_klein_wp.txt. The full paper was read. Separately, SSRN abstract pages (5046463 and 5342477, both confirmed as this paper's working-paper IDs via search) and ScienceDirect (pii S0167268126003343) were blocked by a Cloudflare bot-check under a browser user-agent, the r.jina.ai proxy, and a Googlebot user-agent alike — the author's self-posted PDF substituted for these successfully blocked routes. This is the author's own accepted-version manuscript, not the copy-edited/paginated published PDF carrying the cited DOI, so section/page numbers may differ slightly from the final print version.
verdict: NEW research page (Important tier) — e.g. research/gross-klein-partial-equilibrium-dwl.md — full text was read. Also ENRICH concepts/deadweight-loss.md with a short paragraph flagging that the standard Harberger-triangle exposition assumes other markets are undistorted, an assumption this paper shows is not innocuous.
claim_grade: B-claim for the formal/numerical results (peer-reviewed, accepted at JEBO 2026; full working-paper text read and the key derivations and Table 6 numbers verified directly against it). Tier 1: Till Gross (Carleton University; peer-reviewed record including Journal of Public Economics, American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics, Journal of International Economics, Review of Economic Dynamics — an established academic on public/international finance theory) and Paul Klein (Stockholm University; the paper's title page reads 'In memoriam,' i.e. Klein died before this version's publication — noted here as a fact from the manuscript itself, not independently sourced further, and it should be handled with ordinary editorial sensitivity if repeated on the wiki page).
content_summary: Core result: the traditional deadweight-loss (DWL) formula implicitly assumes the marginal surplus in every other market is zero (i.e., all other markets are perfectly competitive and untaxed). The authors derive an extended formula adding a term that captures the average marginal surplus economy-wide; this term is of the same order of magnitude as the DWL itself and does NOT vanish even as the directly-taxed/monopolized market's size shrinks to a vanishing share of the economy — because although any single other market absorbs only a tiny reallocation of inputs, summed across all other markets the total reallocation is the same order of magnitude as the change in the market under study. Sign-flip result: in a Dixit-Stiglitz numerical example (elasticity of substitution 7, ~1,000,001 markets, 13% goods tax rate) where 90% of markets already carry a commodity tax, taxing one more market actually IMPROVES aggregate welfare (moves the economy toward uniform commodity taxation) even though both the standard DWL and the Goulder & Williams (2003) labour-augmented formula predict a loss — their Table 6 panel (b) shows DWL flat at -0.585 across labour-tax rates while the true general-equilibrium change (their 'GE' column) is positive throughout, +0.11 to +0.46 depending on the labour tax rate. The paper explicitly credits Harberger (1971) with already flagging this gap in principle ('it is in fact rarely done in studies involving applied welfare economics... the sooner it is rectified, the better') and positions itself as supplying the missing tractable partial-equilibrium formula (as against Kaplow's 2021/2023 general-equilibrium treatment, which the authors say reaches similar conclusions by a different route). The authors are explicit that neither the DWL nor their own extended formula is suitable for estimating economy-wide changes in market power or tax structure — only a full general-equilibrium model can do that. Land/rent taxation: a full-text grep for 'land', 'rent tax', and 'Georg' returned zero matches — the paper never discusses land, land value taxation, or Georgist themes; it is a pure produced-goods/labour market-power and commodity-tax analysis. A Georgist implication can be drawn but is NOT made by the authors and must be presented as the wiki's own inference if used: because a land value tax does not change the (perfectly inelastic) quantity of land supplied, the paper's core mechanism — that a market's output change forces input reallocation into or out of other distorted markets — has no analogue for a pure land tax, so this paper's critique targets the Harberger-triangle treatment of ordinary commodity/factor taxes and does not disturb the wiki's existing zero-DWL claim for LVT specifically.
existing_wiki_coverage: concepts/deadweight-loss.md (read in full) currently states the standard Harberger-triangle mechanism, the classical Smith/Pigou antecedents, and Gaffney's attributed land-use-shifting critique of how excess burden is measured — but nowhere states or discusses the 'other markets are undistorted' assumption this paper targets. This is a genuine, non-duplicative gap-fill.
uncertainties: The text read is the authors' own accepted-manuscript PDF (dated June 2025), not the final copy-edited JEBO proof carrying the 2026 DOI — any wiki citation using page/section numbers should note it cites the working-paper version and that minor numbering may differ from the published version. The Georgist-relevance paragraph above is this reviewer's own inference from the paper's mechanism, not a claim the paper makes; a wiki page must attribute it as analysis, not as something Gross & Klein argue. Whether the JEBO published version adds material (e.g., referee-requested robustness checks) beyond this June 2025 draft is unknown.
